title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a model hallucination failure occurring at the output stage of a legal drafting workflow. An AI tool called Irys was used by defense lawyers to assist with legal research and citation, and it generated seven nonexistent case citations, fabricated quotes, and false holdings that appeared across eight court filings. The lawyers believed the tool would verify citations, meaning the failure was compounded by a misunderstanding of what the system actually does, and no independent human check caught the fabrications before the documents were submitted to court.

The failure mode is a model asserting nonexistent legal authority as fact, a well-documented pattern with large language models used for legal research. It happened at the point where AI-generated output moved directly into official filings without verification against an authoritative legal database or manual review by a lawyer who checked each citation at its source. A citator check against any standard legal research service would have identified the nonexistent cases before filing.

What is not established is whether Irys was marketed as a verification tool, whether the lawyers were told it had that capability by the vendor, or whether any sanctions beyond the apology have been imposed in this case.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false holdings in court filings for a lawsuit involving homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga. The homeowner sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable, and subsequent storm damage delayed repairs. Despite efforts to rebuild, the work was never completed, leading Meni-Siliga and her husband to drain savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. A State Farm attorney acknowledged that a colleague used an AI tool called Irys, believing it would verify legal citations, but it failed to catch seven nonexistent case citations across eight filings.

The incident highlights growing concerns about AI use in law, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI. A database tracking legal hallucinations worldwide has documented 1,922 cases, mostly in the United States. Last year, a California attorney received a record ten thousand dollar fine for using ChatGPT in a brief containing fabricated quotes. State Farm stated it expects its external counsel to maintain the highest ethical standards and verify accuracy in all legal filings. The case is scheduled for trial in October.
